title: I was a truck driver when a woman jumped from a moving horse trailer — then I saw what the driver had hidden behind the animals (PART 2)

blocks.text: …get the babies. He signs the papers. He decides who gets to keep them."

Her name was Rosa. She was twenty-four, from a small town outside San Pedro Sula, and she had come north eight months earlier because a woman at a bus station promised her a job as a nanny for a rich family in Dallas. The job turned out to be real, in the worst possible way. She was kept in a series of rented houses and forced to care for small children who arrived and left every few weeks. Babies. Toddlers. Never older than four.

The children were being sold. Not for what I feared when I saw that compartment. For adoption. Wealthy couples who had been turned down by agencies, or didn't want to wait, paid between sixty and ninety thousand dollars for a child with a clean-looking birth certificate and a court decree.

The retired judge, a man who had spent twenty years in family court, produced the decrees. The mothers had been told their babies died, or had been tricked into signing papers in a language they couldn't read.

"There were three with me in the trailer," Rosa said. "Two boys and a little girl. Yesterday they moved them to another truck at the first stop. I jumped because I heard him on the phone. He said I had seen too much."
The first stop on the manifest was a truck stop outside Abilene. The children could be anywhere between there and Oklahoma by now.

I've been driving for twenty-seven years. I know a lot of people who live in their cabs. While the troopers worked their radios, I got on mine and on a group chat of about four hundred long-haul drivers I'd been part of for a decade.
I posted the description Rosa gave me: a white stock trailer with a blue stripe and a Wichita Falls feed-store decal, pulled by a red Dodge dually.
Forty minutes later, a driver named Earl, hauling frozen chicken, answered from a fuel island in Sweetwater. "Got it. Right in front of me. Guy just went inside to pay."

Earl did exactly what I'd asked. He didn't approach. He parked his rig at an angle so the dually couldn't pull out, called 911, and kept talking to the dispatcher until two Nolan County deputies pulled in. They found the children in the back seat of the truck's cab, buckled into car seats, sleepy and hungry but unhurt. The little girl was holding a stuffed horse.
The investigation took the better part of a year. The FBI linked the ring to thirty-one children placed over six years.
The judge was arrested at his ranch on a Tuesday morning; agents found adoption files in his gun safe. Eight others were charged, including the woman from the bus station.

The best part came slowly. DNA testing reunited the two boys with their mother, who had been told in a Houston clinic that her twins were stillborn. The little girl's mother was found in Guatemala and is now living in Texas with her daughter. Some of the older placements are still in the courts, and I won't pretend those stories are simple.

Rosa received a T visa, which protects trafficking survivors who help investigators. She's studying to become a nurse's aide. Every Christmas she sends a card to me and one to Earl, addressed to "the truck drivers."
If you see signs of human trafficking, call the National Human Trafficking Hotline at 1-888-373-7888 or text 233733. Truckers Against Trafficking also offers free training for professional drivers.
